title: How to Help a Doubting Believer
subtitle: On honest doubt, deconstruction, and how a pastor walks with a Christian whose faith has outgrown the easy answers they were given

sections.title: The One Who Stays Behind to Talk
sections.body:
They wait until the room empties. They let the others file out, shake your hand at the door, drive home to lunch. Then they stand there, half turned away, and say the sentence they have been carrying for months. 'I am not sure I believe any of this anymore.'

Your first instinct will be to fix it. Resist that instinct. It is the wrong one.

The person in front of you is not handing you a debate. They are handing you a wound. Somewhere a prayer went unanswered, a child got sick, a marriage went cold, a book asked a question their Sunday school never prepared them to face. The doubt has a history, and the history is rarely the argument they lead with. If you answer the surface question and miss the buried one, you will win the exchange and lose the person. So before you say anything true, make sure they know you are not afraid of them. A doubter has usually already decided the church cannot handle the truth. The first thing your face has to say is that this one can.

sections.title: Honest Doubt Is Not Rebellion
sections.body:
The church has often treated doubt as a sin to be repented of. It is not. There is a doubt that is rebellion dressed up as inquiry, and there is a doubt that is faith trying to stay alive, and a pastor who cannot tell them apart will crush the second while excusing the first.

Thomas wanted to put his hand in the wound. Jesus did not rebuke him. Jesus showed him the wound.

The father in Mark cried out the truest prayer in the Gospels. I believe, help my unbelief. That is not the prayer of an apostate. That is the prayer of a man holding faith and fear in the same hand and refusing to let go of either. Most doubting believers are exactly there. They have not stopped believing. They have stopped pretending. And the pretending was costing them more than the doubt ever could. Honor that. The person who says the quiet part out loud has paid a higher price for honesty than the person who recites the creed without thinking. Do not punish the courage it took to tell you.

sections.title: Give Them Answers, and Admit Where They Run Out
sections.body:
Some doubt is genuinely a question of the mind, and the mind deserves a real answer. If they are wrestling with the resurrection, with suffering, with the trustworthiness of Scripture, do not wave it off with a verse and a smile. Read the hard books with them. Sit with the hard questions long enough that they see you are not flinching.

But answers have a floor. There is a place where the arguments stop and the abyss is still there.

Do not promise that enough apologetics will dissolve every fear. It will not. Faith has always been a bet made in the dark, a trust extended where proof runs out, and the most honest thing you can tell a doubter is that you make that bet too. Tell them what you do with your own unanswered questions. Tell them you have filed certain things in a folder marked 'to be explained later' and gone on following anyway. A doubter does not need a pastor who has never doubted. A doubter needs a pastor who has, and who is still here, kneeling at the same rail, eating the same bread.

sections.title: What Doubt Actually Needs Is Time
sections.body:
Doubt is rarely resolved in a conversation. It is resolved, when it is, over a long obedience that the doubter keeps practicing while the certainty slowly returns or quietly changes shape. Your job is not to end the doubt by Tuesday. Your job is to keep them in the room while the work gets done.

Keep them at the table. Keep them in the songs. Keep them serving someone poorer than themselves.

The believer who stops gathering, stops praying, stops eating with the people of God, will almost always drift, not because the arguments won but because faith starved. Tell them plainly. Do not solve your doubt alone in a dark room at midnight with the internet. Solve it in the light, among people, over time. And then keep showing up for them. Text them on a Thursday. Ask how it sits this week. The doubter who knows one pastor will not let go of them has a thread back, and people have walked all the way home on a thinner thread than that.

sections.title: Why Their Doubt Frightens You
sections.body:
Here is the part no one says from the platform. The reason a doubter unsettles you is that they are asking out loud the questions you have buried. Their honesty exposes your performance. Their wound presses on yours.

I have sat across from a doubting man and felt my own faith wobble in the chair. I did not let it show. That was the cowardice.

A pastor who has never sat in the dark himself will manage doubters from a safe distance and call it strength. It is not strength. It is fear wearing a collar. The shepherds who help doubters are the ones who have been lost in the same field, who know the cold of it, who can say me too and mean it. So do your own work. Find the place where you have outsourced your faith to your job and never tested whether you would believe it if no one paid you to. Then go back to the one who waited after the service. They do not need you to be certain. They need you to be honest, which is the one thing your title cannot do for you and the only thing that will help them.
